title: Short Stuff: Brazilian Jars
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Brazilian jars: Roman amphorae reportedly found on the seabed of Guanabara Bay near Rio de Janeiro. Fishermen snagged jars in their nets; diver Jose Alvares Cabral... (see note) Jose Alvares Shara, actually transcribed as Jose Two Shara, brought two up in 1976. Underwater archaeologist Robert Marx later dove the site, found about 200 amphorae about 90 feet down, and linked them to a third-century Roman-era kiln site at Kasr el Ouadi-like Morocco location (transcribed as Kas Ko, Coas), with UMass expert Elizabeth Will (transcribed as Elizabeth Will) confirming the design. Marx theorized a Roman ship was blown off course and wrecked. The Brazilian government, navy, and authorities shut down his work and banned him; he was accused of plundering and black market sales, which he denied. Later, Americo Santarelli, a free diver and amphora collector, claimed he had planted sixteen replica amphorae in the bay in the 1960s to age them, casting doubt on the whole find. Hosts also mention Kevin Pollock, Usual Suspects actor and Alchemy improv show participant, in a closing tangent.

segments.title: Opening banter and Hamona hammana
segments.summary: Hosts open the short episode with banter about the phrase 'hamona hammana' and its possible vaudeville origins, then introduce Brazil's first European landing.

segments.title: Discovery of the jars
segments.summary: Cabral's landing in Brazil is introduced. Fishermen near Guanabara Bay snag jars in their nets, and in 1976 diver Jose Shara brings two to the surface. The navy takes them and they draw the attention of Robert Marx.

segments.title: Marx's dive and Roman amphorae identification
segments.summary: Marx identifies the jars as Roman amphorae and dives about 90 feet down, finding roughly 200 amphorae spread over about three tennis courts. UMass expert Elizabeth Will traces them to a third-century site in Morocco. Marx theorizes a Roman ship was wrecked near Rio.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the discussion of Brazil's response.

segments.title: Brazil's response and Marx's ban
segments.summary: Brazilian authorities shut down Marx's excavation, the navy covered the site with fill dirt, and he was banned from Brazil and accused of plundering and black market sales. Marx had a strong reputation, including UNESCO work and knighthoods.

segments.title: Santarelli's replica claim and doubts
segments.summary: Free diver Americo Santarelli claims the amphorae were replicas he planted sixteen of in the 1960s to age them. The hosts note that most of the evidence comes from Marx and that Marx later dropped the subject.

segments.title: Kevin Pollock tangent and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts shout out Kevin Pollock, Usual Suspects actor and Alchemy improv performer, then sign off with a production credit.
